mainTopic: Extra wording that adds a לאו for taking millstones as collateral, counting liability for working pairs, and whether holding a seized slaughtering knife lets a lender claim his debt.
overview: This amud opens in the middle of an answer. The גמרא explains why the phrase ״כִּי נֶפֶשׁ הוּא חֹבֵל״ counts as an extra לאו for the millstones: the words are extra in the verse. By קרבן פסח, ״כִּי אִם צְלִי אֵשׁ״ is different, because a ברייתא needs those words for another teaching. Two ברייתות then discuss taking a pair of tools as collateral. The first supports רב יהודה: a full pair brings two sets of מלקות, and one piece alone brings one. The second learns from ריחיים ורכב that any two separate tools doing one job bring a liability for each. Next comes a real case of a slaughtering knife taken as collateral. אביי says to return it and go to court, while רבא says the lender can claim up to the knife's value. The גמרא shows that both accept רב הונא בר אבין's rule that holding an item usually lent or rented gives no credibility. They argue only about whether people lend slaughtering knives. The amud ends with הדרן עלך, closing פרק המקבל.

steps.title: The general verse is extra, so it is applied to the millstones
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its answer: the phrase ״כִּי נֶפֶשׁ הוּא חֹבֵל״ is extra, so it becomes another prohibition on the millstones.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is extra. Since it is extra, apply it to the lower and upper millstones.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer that started on the previous page. It says the general phrase in the verse is extra, so we apply it as one more prohibition on the millstones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A general לאו (לאו שבכללות) normally does not bring its own מלקות. Here, though, the phrase is not needed for anything else. So the extra wording is read as a real added prohibition on ריחיים ורכב.

keyTerms.meaning: extra, not needed for anything else in the verse
throw it, apply it (to another case)
the lower and upper millstones

phrases.english: It is superfluous,
phrases.notes: "It" is the phrase ״כִּי נֶפֶשׁ הוּא חֹבֵל״ (דברים 24:6) from the discussion just before this.

phrases.english: since it is superfluous –
apply it to the lower and upper millstones.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the answer to the challenge from the previous page, which said the general phrase is only a לאו שבכללות.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual: the general phrase is extra in the verse, so it counts as its own prohibition.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A general לאו should not bring its own מלקות.
steps.terutzMaskana: Because this general phrase is extra, it is applied to the millstones as another לאו.

steps.title: Why roasting the קרבן פסח is different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why the case of ״כִּי אִם צְלִי אֵשׁ״ by קרבן פסח does not work the same way: there the phrase is needed for a different teaching.
steps.simpleTranslation: But here, "but roasted with fire" is not extra, because it is needed for what a ברייתא teaches: when a person is included in the command to eat it roasted, he is included in the ban on eating it raw. When he is not included in the command to eat it roasted, he is not included in the ban on eating it raw.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets the millstone case apart from the קרבן פסח case. There, the words ״כִּי אִם צְלִי אֵשׁ״ are not extra, so they cannot be used to turn the general לאו of eating it raw or cooked into separate לאוין that bring separate מלקות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban on eating the קרבן פסח raw or cooked is a general לאו, and the phrase ״כִּי אִם צְלִי אֵשׁ״ could have been read as extra wording that splits it into separate לאוין. But that phrase is needed to link the ban on eating it raw (נא) to the time of the מצוה of eating it roasted. Since it already has a job, it is not extra, so the ban stays a general לאו with no added מלקות. The millstone phrase has no other job, so it is different.

keyTerms.meaning: roasted over fire (how the קרבן פסח must be eaten)
"arise and eat," a positive command to eat
the ban on eating it raw or half-cooked
he needs it (for another teaching)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two cases. In both, a general לאו is involved. Only in the millstone case is there truly extra wording (״כִּי נֶפֶשׁ הוּא חֹבֵל״) to treat as its own prohibition. By קרבן פסח, the possible extra wording (״כִּי אִם צְלִי אֵשׁ״) is needed for another teaching.
steps.whatToRemember: A general phrase gives an added לאו only when it is truly extra. If it is needed for another teaching, as ״כִּי אִם צְלִי אֵשׁ״ is, it does not.

phrases.english: But here, "but roasted with fire"
is not superfluous,
as he needs it for that which is taught in a ברייתא:
At the time when one is included in "arise, eat it roasted,"
he is included in "do not eat it raw."
At a time when one is not included in "arise, eat it roasted" –
he is not included in "do not eat it raw."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the answer by explaining why the case used in the challenge (קרבן פסח) does not match the millstone case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: one phrase is extra, the other is needed for a separate teaching.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: ״כִּי אִם צְלִי אֵשׁ״ also looks extra, so by the same logic it should be used to give separate מלקות for eating the קרבן פסח raw. That would contradict the rule that the general לאו there brings no מלקות.
steps.terutzMaskana: That phrase is needed to tie the ban on eating raw to the time of the מצוה, so it is not extra. The millstone phrase is extra.

steps.title: A ברייתא that supports רב יהודה
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that taking a pair of tools as collateral brings two sets of מלקות, and one piece alone brings only one.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא was taught in line with רב יהודה: If one took a barbers' scissors or a pair of cows as collateral, he is liable for two. If he took this one alone or that one alone, he is liable for only one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the argument about the millstones. It brings a ברייתא that fits רב יהודה's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gives only two sets of מלקות for the full pair. It does not add another one for the general verse. That matches רב יהודה, who does not count the general phrase as an added לאו.

keyTerms.meaning: a ברייתא was taught that supports him
took as collateral (a pledge for a loan)
barbers' scissors, made of two blades
a pair of cows that plow together

phrases.english: It is taught in a ברייתא in accordance with רב יהודה:
If one took as collateral barbers' scissors
or a pair of cows –
he is liable for two.
This one by itself or that one by itself –
phrases.notes: This means taking just one blade or just one cow.

phrases.english: he is liable for only one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the argument between רב הונא and רב יהודה and brings support for רב יהודה.
steps.raayaObject: רב יהודה's view that a pair brings only two sets of מלקות, not an extra one for the general verse.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about barbers' scissors and a pair of cows.

steps.title: Learning from the millstones: two tools for one job bring two liabilities
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא uses the verse about ריחיים ורכב to teach that any two separate tools that work together on one job bring a separate liability for each.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another ברייתא teaches: If one took barbers' scissors or a pair of cows as collateral, you might think he is liable for only one. So the verse says, "He may not take the lower and upper millstone as collateral." Lower and upper millstones are two separate tools that do one job, and one is liable for each on its own. So too, any two separate tools that do one job bring a liability for each on its own.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא. It shows where the rule of two liabilities for a pair comes from.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone might think a pair that does one job counts as one item and brings only one liability. The ברייתא learns from ריחיים ורכב that two separate tools stay two, even when they work together. It then applies this to scissors, cows, and anything like them.

keyTerms.meaning: one might have thought
so the verse teaches
one job or task
separately, on its own

steps.whatToRemember: Two separate tools that work together on one job are still two items. Taking both as collateral brings a separate liability for each. This is learned from ריחיים ורכב.
steps.whyThisMatters: The millstone verse is turned into a general rule for every working pair, not just millstones.

phrases.english: And it is taught in another ברייתא:
If one took as collateral barbers' scissors
or a pair of cows,

phrases.aramaic: יָכוֹל לֹא יְהֵא חַיָּיב אֶלָּא אַחַת –
phrases.english: one might think he is liable for only one –
so the verse states: "He may not take as collateral the lower and upper millstone."
Just as the lower and upper millstones are distinct
in that they are two tools and do one job,
and one is liable for this one separately
and for that one separately –
so too, all items that are
two distinct tools
and do one job –
he is liable for this one separately
and for that one separately.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second ברייתא that gives the verse source for counting each tool in a pair separately.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that each tool in a working pair brings its own liability.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The verse ״לֹא יַחֲבֹל רֵיחַיִם וָרָכֶב״, as explained in the ברייתא.

steps.title: A slaughtering knife taken as collateral: אביי says return it and go to court
steps.stepSummary: A man took a slaughtering knife as collateral. אביי rules that he must return it, since it is a food-making tool, and then sue for his money in court.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man took a slaughtering knife from his fellow as collateral. He came before אביי. אביי told him: Go give it back, because it is a tool used to make food. Then go to court about the debt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real-life case that applies the earlier rule about not taking food-making tools as collateral. אביי gives his ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A slaughtering knife is used to prepare meat, so it belongs to the same group as the millstones from the earlier steps. אביי says the lender gets no benefit from holding it. He must return it and prove his debt in court like anyone else.

keyTerms.meaning: A slaughtering knife
A tool used to prepare food, which is forbidden to take as collateral
Stand in judgment, meaning go to court

phrases.english: A certain man who took as collateral
a slaughtering knife from his fellow.
He came before Abaye.
He said to him: Go, return it,

phrases.aramaic: דְּהָוֵי לֵיהּ כְּלִי שֶׁעוֹשִׂים בּוֹ אוֹכֶל נֶפֶשׁ,
phrases.english: since it is a tool used to prepare food,
and come stand in judgment about it.
phrases.notes: He means: sue the borrower in court to prove how much he owes you.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דַּחֲבַל סַכִּינָא דְּאַשְׁכַּבְתָּא מֵחַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the earlier rule about food-making tools to a new real-life case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אביי: a slaughtering knife must be returned, and the lender must prove his debt in court.

steps.title: רבא: no need for court, he can claim up to the knife's value
steps.stepSummary: רבא disagrees. Holding the knife lets the lender claim his debt up to the knife's value without a full court case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: He does not need to go to court over it. He can claim up to its value.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a different ruling on the same case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא holds that because the knife is in the lender's hands, he is believed about the debt, up to what the knife is worth. אביי gave him no such advantage. This difference is what the rest of the sugya explains.

keyTerms.meaning: To claim, meaning to state how much he is owed
Up to their value, meaning as much as the item is worth

phrases.english: Rava said: He does not need
to stand in judgment about it,
and he can claim up to their value.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: לָא צְרִיךְ לְמֵיקַם בְּדִינָא עֲלֵהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with אביי's ruling on the same case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא: holding the item lets the lender claim his debt up to its value.

steps.title: Why does אביי reject this? The goats case says the opposite
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges אביי from a case in נהרדעא: goats ate someone's barley, he seized them, and אבוה דשמואל ruled he can claim up to their value.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does אביי not hold that reasoning? How is this different from the goats that ate peeled barley in נהרדעא? The barley's owner came and seized them and claimed a large amount. אבוה דשמואל said he can claim up to their value!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why אביי does not accept רבא's reasoning, when an earlier authority clearly used it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the goats case, holding the goats let the barley owner claim his loss up to their value, which is exactly רבא's idea. So why would אביי give the knife-holder no such credibility? The two cases look the same.

keyTerms.meaning: Goats
Peeled barley
The father of שמואל, who served as a judge
What is different? A way of asking why two cases are treated differently

phrases.english: And does Abaye not hold that reasoning?
How is it different from those goats
that ate peeled barley in Neharde'a,
and the owner of the barley came and seized them,
and was claiming a large amount?
And Shmuel's father said
he can claim up to their value!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי using an earlier ruling that matches רבא.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's ruling that the lender gets no credibility from holding the knife
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: אבוה דשמואל gave credibility up to the item's value to someone holding goats, so the knife-holder should get the same.

steps.title: Goats are not lent out, but knives are
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers for אביי: goats are not normally lent or rented, but a knife is, so holding a knife does not show anything.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, goats are not something usually lent out or rented. Here, a knife is something usually lent out or rented.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends אביי by pointing out a real difference between goats and a knife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Holding an item only gives you credibility if it suggests the item could really be yours. People do not usually lend goats, so having them is meaningful. People often lend knives, so having one may just mean you borrowed it, and it gives no credibility.

keyTerms.meaning: To lend out and to rent out
There (the other case) / here (our case)

phrases.english: There, it is not an item that is usually
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. The meaning is the same.

phrases.english: lent out or rented.
Here, it is an item that is usually
lent out or rented.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָתָם לָאו מִידֵּי דַּעֲבִיד לְאוֹשׁוֹלֵי וּלְאוֹגוֹרֵי הוּא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Holding any item gives credibility up to its value, so the knife should work like the goats.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only items not usually lent give credibility. A knife is usually lent, so it gives none.
steps.confusionAlert: אביי agrees with the goats ruling. He only says a knife is a different kind of item.

steps.title: Support from רב הונא בר אבין: holding a lendable item proves nothing
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא בר אבין ruled that if someone holds an item that is usually lent or rented and says he bought it, he is not believed.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב הונא בר אבין sent: For items that are usually lent or rented, if the holder says, 'They were bought by me,' he is not believed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings an outside ruling to support the difference it just made.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually, whoever holds an item is believed if he says he bought it. That is why he can also claim a debt up to its value, since he could have just claimed the item is his. With lendable items even a claim of 'I bought it' is not believed, so holding them gives no credibility for a debt either.

keyTerms.meaning: Items that are usually lent out and rented
They were bought by me
He is not believed

steps.whatToRemember: Holding an item gives you credibility only if it is not the kind of item people usually lend or rent out.

phrases.english: As Rav Huna bar Avin sent:
Items that are usually lent out or rented,
and he says, 'They were bought by me':
he is not believed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer given in step 8.
steps.raayaObject: The difference between lendable and non-lendable items
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ruling sent by רב הונא בר אבין
steps.whyThisMatters: This rule about lendable items is the key to both sides of the sugya. The only question left is whether a knife counts as one.

steps.title: Doesn't רבא himself accept the rule about lendable items?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא: he himself took wool shears and an אגדה scroll away from orphans because they are items that are usually lent.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבא not hold this reasoning? But רבא took wool shears and an אגדה scroll away from orphans, because they are items usually lent out or rented!
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא turns to רבא and asks why he ignores the rule about lendable items in the knife case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא clearly accepts רב הונא בר אבין's rule, since he used it to take items away from orphans. So why does he give the knife-holder credibility, when a knife seems to be lendable too?

keyTerms.meaning: A pair of wool shears
A scroll of אגדה
Orphans
He took out, meaning he took the items out of their possession

phrases.english: And does Rava not hold this reasoning?
But Rava took away
wool shears and a scroll of aggada
from orphans, as items that are usually
lent out or rented!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending אביי, the גמרא now challenges רבא with the same rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's ruling that the knife-holder can claim up to its value
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבא himself applied the rule about lendable items. A knife seems lendable, so he should agree with אביי.

steps.title: רבא: people do not lend slaughtering knives, because they get damaged
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that a slaughtering knife is not a lendable item, because it easily gets nicked, so owners are careful not to lend it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא could tell you: This one too, since it gets damaged, people are particular and do not lend it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers for רבא. He agrees with the rule but says a slaughtering knife does not fall under it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי and רבא both accept רב הונא בר אבין's rule. They only disagree about the facts: אביי sees a knife as a usual item to lend, and רבא sees it as something people refuse to lend because a small nick ruins it for slaughtering. So for רבא the knife is like the goats, and holding it gives credibility.

keyTerms.meaning: Gets nicked or damaged
People are particular, meaning careful with their things
He could say to you. The גמרא answers for an אמורא

steps.whatToRemember: אביי and רבא agree on the rule about lendable items. They argue only about whether a slaughtering knife is something people lend.

phrases.english: Rava could say to you:
This one too, since it gets damaged,
people are particular and do not lend it.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: the knife is not a lendable item
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A slaughtering knife is a usual item to lend, so רבא should not give the holder credibility.
steps.terutzMaskana: People do not lend slaughtering knives because they get damaged, so holding one does give credibility up to its value.

steps.title: Hadran — Closing פרק המקבל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the chapter called המקבל with the traditional closing line, הדרן עלך.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, chapter המקבל.
steps.whatsHappening: The learning of this chapter is done, and the text marks the ending with a short farewell line. This is not part of the back-and-forth argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הדרן עלך means 'we will return to you.' It shows love for the learning and a promise to come back and review it. The chapter is called המקבל because that is its first word.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you, the traditional formula said when finishing a chapter
The one who receives (a field to work), the name of this chapter, taken from its first word
A chapter of the משנה and גמרא

steps.whatToRemember: פרק המקבל is finished. Its last sugya taught that a person holding an item that is usually lent or rented is not believed when he says he bought it. It also taught that a slaughtering knife does not count as such an item, because owners are careful not to lend it.

phrases.english: We will return to you, chapter HaMekabel

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Comes after רבא's answer in step 11 that a slaughtering knife is not a lendable item, which ends the chapter's last sugya.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The chapter המקבל is complete, and we commit to returning to review it.
